title: Write the case study before you ask the client
description: Write the case study before you ask the client. Draft it from what you've got, then choose: client sign-off, or publish it unbranded.
dek: Draft the case study from the proposal and the project notes, then decide if a name goes on it.
author: Shane Kennedy

video.title: Write the case study first. Marketing for IT firms

images.alt: “Write the case study first” in bold capitals, beside a man reading a document

shortVersion: A lot of teams think they need a client's permission before they start writing a case study, so it's left on the to-do list for months.
Proof and testimonials are a key part of buying. If a buyer finds client stories on a competitor's site and none on yours, who are they going to choose?
Draft it from what you've got. Then send it to the client for sign-off, or remove the branding and publish it unbranded.

beats.heading: Waiting for permission
body: A lot of teams think you need permission from a client before you even start writing the case study.
So the case studies sit on the to-do list for months, and the website shows no logos and no customer stories.
Asking first also hands the client a job: find time for an interview, read a draft, then approve it. A client can be happy to help and still not get round to it.

steps.text: It sits on the to-do list
No logos and no customer stories on the website

beats.heading: What the buyer compares
body: Proof and testimonials are such a key part of the buying process that if a buyer goes to your website, or to a competitor who has this down pat, who are they going to choose?
They're comparing firms they've never worked with. A story about a client like them is the closest they'll get to trying you out first.

beats.heading: The raw material you already have
body: You already have so many case studies sitting there, and so much raw material you can pull from.
It's all in the original proposal, the project notes and the emails from the first few weeks, and pulling those together gives you the bones of a first draft.
For your best clients, elaborate on the problem they had when they started with you, and then the objective you helped them hit.

graphic.prompt: Pick one of your best clients. Can you write down…
items: The problem they had when they started with you
The objective you helped them hit
graphic.privacyNote: Nothing you tick is stored or sent.

beats.heading: Then choose: sign-off or unbranded
body: Once you've drafted it, you've got two options. You can send it to the customer, get sign-off and post it. Or you can remove all the branding and publish it as an unbranded case study.

items.title: Option 1: sign-off
items.text: Send it to the client, then post it

items.title: Option 2: unbranded
items.text: Remove the branding and publish it

beats.heading: Why unbranded can be a good thing
body: Anonymity is actually a good thing, especially if you're in cyber security. It does show that you protect your clients.
There's a lot an unbranded story can still say. Name the industry, the size of the business and the problem. Leave out anything a reader could use to work out who it's about.

take.key: and then decide if a name goes onto it.
body: Case studies are part of Centurion, the strategy we run with IT firms.
